tip: Italian expresses hunger with avere (to have), not essere: ho fame is literally I have hunger.
For feeling hot a person uses avere: abbiamo caldo. Weather uses fare instead: fa caldo.
Language names are written lowercase in Italian: italiano, never Italiano.
Verbs like capire insert -isc- in most present forms: capiscono, not capono.
After a modal like potere the next verb stays in the infinitive: possiamo aiutare.
Being careful or alert uses stare, not essere: stai attento.
amico has an irregular plural, amici, pronounced with a soft c.
Health and how you feel use stare, not essere: stiamo benissimo.
Informal tu commands of -ere and -ire verbs use the present tense form: bevi = drink.
Italian uses the present tense for scheduled future events: partite domani = you leave tomorrow.
dire is irregular; the noi form is diciamo, not dicamo.
lo and la shorten to l' before a vowel: l'acqua.
Verbs ending in -gare add an h before -i to keep the hard g: paghiamo.
Feminine una drops to un' before a vowel: un'insalata. Masculine un never takes an apostrophe.
autobus is invariable: L'autobus is singular, gli autobus plural, spelled the same.
chiamarsi is reflexive; ti chiami literally means you call yourself.
Age uses avere, not essere: hai ... anni is literally how many years you have.
aspettare already means to wait for, so no per follows it: aspetti l'autobus.
da plus l' contracts to dall': dall'autobus.
Adjectives ending in -e use one form for both genders: pesante for masculine or feminine.
Italian uses the article, not a possessive, for body parts: i capelli = her hair.
arancione ends in -e, so it changes only for number: arancioni in the plural, either gender.
bere has an irregular past participle, bevuto, not beruto.
Yes/no questions keep normal word order; only rising tone marks them: Hai pagato il conto?
magari plus a past subjunctive expresses a wish: smettesse = if only it would stop.
Possessives normally take the definite article: la mia macchina, literally the my car.
Form comparatives by putting più before the adjective: più leggera = lighter.
Before an adjective molto means very and never changes form: molto dolce.
suonare is the verb for playing instruments: suonare il pianoforte. Games use giocare.
palazzo usually means a building or apartment block, not a palace.
fa means ago and comes after the time expression: due giorni fa = two days ago.
Object pronouns attach to an infinitive, which drops its final -e: dire plus ti becomes dirti.
bello shortens to bel before a masculine noun: bel tramonto.
dei, from di plus i, means some before a masculine plural noun: dei fiori.
simpatico means nice or likeable, not sympathetic.
The article with a weekday means every one of them: il lunedì = on Mondays.
